claim: HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp160 is targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by its signal peptide during synthesis.
source: Like all other secretory proteins, the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp160 is targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by its signal peptide during synthesis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about secretory protein targeting.

claim: Proper gp160 folding in the ER requires core glycosylation, disulfide-bond formation and proline isomerization.
source: Proper gp160 folding in the ER requires core glycosylation, disulfide-bond formation and proline isomerization.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Signal-peptide cleavage of gp160 occurs only late after gp160 chain termination.
source: Signal-peptide cleavage occurs only late after gp160 chain termination and is dependent on folding of the soluble subunit gp120 to a near-native conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Signal-peptide cleavage of gp160 is dependent on folding of the soluble subunit gp120 to a near-native conformation.
source: Signal-peptide cleavage occurs only late after gp160 chain termination and is dependent on folding of the soluble subunit gp120 to a near-native conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that preventing proper folding blocks cleavage.

claim: Conserved residues from the signal peptide and residues downstream of the canonical cleavage site form an extended alpha-helix in the ER membrane.
source: Conserved residues from the signal peptide and residues downstream of the canonical cleavage site form an extended alpha-helix in the ER membrane, which covers the cleavage site, thus preventing cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural predictions and experimental data in the results section.

claim: The extended alpha-helix covers the cleavage site, thus preventing cleavage.
source: Conserved residues from the signal peptide and residues downstream of the canonical cleavage site form an extended alpha-helix in the ER membrane, which covers the cleavage site, thus preventing cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural predictions and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: A point mutation in the signal peptide (M26P) breaks the alpha helix allowing co-translational cleavage.
source: A point mutation in the signal peptide breaks the alpha helix allowing co-translational cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 7.

claim: Postponed cleavage of gp160 enhances functional folding of the molecule.
source: We demonstrate that postponed cleavage of gp160 enhances functional folding of the molecule.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by conformational analysis and infectivity assays.

claim: The change to early cleavage results in decreased viral fitness compared to wild-type HIV.
source: The change to early cleavage results in decreased viral fitness compared to wild-type HIV.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by competition assays in Figure 8.

claim: Cleavable signal peptides are variable in sequence but share characteristics of an N-terminal region with typically 0–2 basic residues, a membrane-spanning hydrophobic α-helix (H) region, and a C-terminal region that often contains a signal-peptide cleavage site.
source: Cleavable signal peptides are variable in sequence but share characteristics of an N-terminal region with typically 0–2 basic residues, a membrane-spanning hydrophobic α-helix (H) region, and a C-terminal region that often contains a signal-peptide cleavage site (von Heijne, 1983; von Heijne, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Signal peptides are widely believed to be cleaved co-translationally.
source: Signal peptides are widely believed to be cleaved co-translationally (Blobel and Dobberstein, 1975; Jackson and Blobel, 1977; Martoglio and Dobberstein, 1998), but cleavage may well occur anywhere from early co-translational to late post-translational, depending on the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The minimal requirement for cleavage is the emergence of the cleavage site in the ER lumen, which translates to ~70 synthesized residues of a nascent polypeptide chain.
source: The minimal requirement for cleavage is the emergence of the cleavage site in the ER lumen, which translates to ~70 synthesized residues of a nascent polypeptide chain (Daniels et al., 2003; Kowarik et al., 2002; Hou et al., 2012), and its recognition by the signal-peptidase complex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The gp160 signal peptide acts as a membrane tether for at least 15 min after synthesis.
source: The gp160 signal peptide acts as a membrane tether for at least 15 min after synthesis and requires at least some folding of the ectodomain for cleavage (Land et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When proper folding is prevented by maintaining gp160 in a reduced state with DTT treatment or by blocking N-linked glycosylation using tunicamycin, the signal remains uncleaved and gp160 fails to exit the ER.
source: When proper folding is prevented by maintaining gp160 in a reduced state with DTT treatment or by blocking N-linked glycosylation using tunicamycin, the signal remains uncleaved and gp160 fails to exit the ER (Land et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Gp160 begins as a transmembrane protein whose folding requires formation of conserved disulfide bonds, abundant glycosylation, proline isomerization, and trimerization before the protein leaves the ER.
source: Gp160 begins as a transmembrane protein whose folding requires formation of conserved disulfide bonds, abundant glycosylation, proline isomerization, and trimerization before the protein leaves the ER (Land et al., 2003; Willey et al., 1988; Earl et al., 1990; Earl et al., 1991; Land and Braakman, 2001; van Anken et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the Golgi complex, gp160 glycans are modified and furin proteases cleave the trimeric glycoprotein into its two subunits, which stay non-covalently attached and are incorporated into new virions at the plasma membrane.
source: In the Golgi complex, gp160 glycans are modified and furin proteases cleave the trimeric glycoprotein into its two subunits, which stay non-covalently attached and are incorporated into new virions at the plasma membrane (Araújo and Almeida, 2013; Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Gp160 is essential for virus entry as gp120 recognizes CD4, the HIV receptor on the cell surface, and one of the HIV coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4, whereas gp41 mediates fusion with the target membrane.
source: Gp160 is essential for virus entry as gp120 recognizes CD4, the HIV receptor on the cell surface, and one of the HIV coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4, whereas gp41 mediates fusion with the target membrane (Blumenthal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The soluble subunit gp120 dominates gp160 folding and can fold and be secreted on its own, in the absence of gp41.
source: The soluble subunit gp120 dominates gp160 folding and can fold and be secreted on its own, in the absence of gp41 (Land et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Signal-peptide cleavage of gp120 is similarly delayed as for full-length gp160 and obeys the same rules.
source: Signal-peptide cleavage of gp120 is similarly delayed as for full-length gp160 and obeys the same rules (Land et al., 2003; van Anken et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Replacement of the natural gp160 signal peptide with unrelated signal peptides (HA, cystatin, Igκ, optimal, or suboptimal) results in co-translational cleavage.
source: After completion of synthesis, unprocessed deglycosylated gp120, with its signal peptide still attached (Ru) runs as a single band of ~70 kDa (Land et al., 2003) (Figure 1A). After a 60-min chase, a second band with increased mobility appears, representing signal-peptide-cleaved gp120 (Rc). In contrast, immediately after synthesis all gp120 constructs with non-native signal peptides already ran as a single band at the position of signal-peptide-cleaved gp120, indicating that the gp120 signal peptide is necessary for delayed signal cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1A with pulse-chase analysis.

claim: The gp120 signal peptide is necessary for delayed signal cleavage.
source: In contrast, immediately after synthesis all gp120 constructs with non-native signal peptides already ran as a single band at the position of signal-peptide-cleaved gp120, indicating that the gp120 signal peptide is necessary for delayed signal cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The gp120 signal peptide alone is not sufficient for post-translational cleavage.
source: The HA-signal-peptide construct (HA-gp120) again was detected as co-translationally cleaved gp120 (Figure 1B). The gp120 signal peptide alone hence did not convert HA into a post-translationally cleaved protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Features of both mature gp120 and its signal peptide are necessary for post-translational cleavage.
source: Therefore, features of both mature gp120 and its signal peptide are necessary for post-translational cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the signal peptide swap experiments.

claim: Gp160 residues downstream of the signal cleavage site, in combination with the signal peptide itself, are sufficient to modulate cleavage efficiency of the gp160 signal peptide.
source: We concluded that gp160 residues downstream of the signal cleavage site, in combination with the signal peptide itself, were sufficient to modulate cleavage efficiency of the gp160 signal peptide.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Addition of ~10 gp160 residues downstream of the signal peptide turns the signal peptide into a predominantly uncleaved signal anchor.
source: Processing decreased even more with additional gp160 residues and the inclusion of ~10 downstream residues turned the signal peptide into a predominantly uncleaved signal anchor.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The amino acids responsible for the switch from signal peptide to signal anchor (+4 to +10) are highly conserved across all HIV-1 subtypes.
source: The amino acids responsible for the switch from signal peptide to signal anchor (Figure 2AB, +4 to +10) were shown to be highly conserved across all subtypes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: An alignment of more than 4100 sequences shows 99–100% conservation of amino acids at positions +4 to +10, with the exception of L34 which was 89% conserved.
source: Indeed, an alignment of more than 4100 sequences shows 99–100% conservation of these amino acids, with the exception of L34 which was 89% conserved (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Post-translational signal-peptide cleavage is a conserved phenomenon across HIV-1 subtypes.
source: Nevertheless, we concluded that post-translational signal-peptide cleavage is a conserved phenomenon across HIV-1 subtypes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experiments with subtype C isolate 93IN101.

claim: Signal-peptide-cleaved GFP (SP+1) diffused rapidly (D = 9.6 ± 2.7 µm/s2), comparable with the ER-GFP control (D = 10.2 ± 1.6 µm/s2) and indicative of a soluble protein.
source: Signal-peptide-cleaved GFP (Figure 4B, SP+1) diffused rapidly (D = 9.6 ± 2.7 µm/s2), comparable with the ER-GFP control (D = 10.2 ± 1.6 µm/s2) and indicative of a soluble protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Addition of ten gp160 residues downstream of the cleavage site to GFP (SP+10) resulted in a much lower diffusion coefficient (D = 1.7 ± 0.6 µm/s2).
source: Addition of ten gp160 residues downstream of the cleavage site to GFP (SP+10) slowed signal-peptide cleavage dramatically and resulted in a much lower D (D = 1.7 ± 0.6 µm/s2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Uncleaved SP+10 GFP was fully integrated in the membrane and not in the translocon protein channel.
source: Signal-cleaved SP+10 was fully soluble, while uncleaved SP+10 GFP was only found in the pellet fraction, indicating that it was fully integrated in the membrane and not in the translocon protein channel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by carbonate extraction in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of a minimum of 5 to 10 gp120 amino acids downstream of the cleavage site prevented co-translational signal-peptide cleavage and anchored GFP to the membrane through this signal peptide.
source: Thus, the presence of a minimum of 5 to 10 gp120 amino acids downstream of the cleavage site prevented co-translational signal-peptide cleavage an anchored GFP to the membrane through this signal peptide.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FRAP and carbonate extraction data.

claim: Position 41 of gp160 is located 11–12 residues away from the membrane-water interface.
source: Glycosylation of the second site sharply increased at position 41 and beyond, which thus is located 11–12 residues away from the membrane-water interface.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by glycosylation mapping in Figure 5.

claim: The cleavage site of gp160's signal peptide is at the membrane-lumen interface, with T31 barely exposed in the ER lumen.
source: This result strongly supports the interpretation that the cleavage site of gp160's signal peptide is at the membrane-lumen interface, with T31 barely exposed in the ER lumen.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from glycosylation mapping data.

claim: The shielding of the cleavage site by membrane phospholipids contributes to the delayed cleavage of the signal peptide.
source: It therefore is likely that the shielding of the cleavage site by membrane phospholipids contributes to the delayed cleavage of the signal peptide.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the location of the cleavage site at the membrane interface.

claim: The gp160 signal peptide contains a predicted hydrophobic H-region that overlaps substantially with the C-region containing the cleavage site.
source: In contrast, gp160's signal peptide contains a predicted hydrophobic H-region that overlaps substantially with the C-region containing the cleavage site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown by SignalP analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: The probabilities for the gp160 signal peptide to be a cleavable signal peptide or an uncleaved signal anchor were 0.628 and 0.358, respectively.
source: The probabilities for the gp160 signal peptide to be a cleavable signal peptide or an uncleaved signal anchor were 0.628 and 0.358, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and derived from SignalP analysis.

claim: The majority of transmembrane-domain prediction algorithms suggested that residues 33 up to 44 of gp160 form an extended alpha helix.
source: Indeed, the majority of transmembrane-domain prediction algorithms suggested that residues 33 up to 44 of gp160 form an extended alpha helix (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: De novo structure predictions using Robetta show the alpha helix overlapping with the cleavage site.
source: De novo structure predictions using Robetta (Kim et al., 2004) also show the alpha helix overlapping with the cleavage site (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutation M26P increased signal-peptide cleavage probability from 0.628 to 0.928 and clearly separated H- and C-regions.
source: SignalP analysis revealed that mutation M26P increased signal-peptide cleavage probability from 0.628 to 0.928 and clearly separated H- and C-regions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: De novo structure predictions showed a break in alpha-helical structure around the cleavage site for M26P mutant.
source: Similarly, de novo structure predictions also showed a break in alpha-helical structure around the cleavage site (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: M26P gp160 signal peptide is cleaved co-translationally.
source: Immediately after synthesis M26P gp160 already ran primarily as a single band in the position of signal-peptide-cleaved gp160 (Figure 7A, Cells R). As predicted, cleavage occurred co-translationally.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by pulse-chase analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: M26P gp160 takes as long as wild-type gp160 to fold and exit the ER.
source: Even though M26P gp160 signal peptide was rapidly removed, the mutant took as long as wild-type gp160 to fold and exit the ER.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by pulse-chase data in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-translational signal-peptide cleavage of M26P gp160 significantly altered the oxidative folding pathway; folding intermediates acquired high compactness more quickly during synthesis.
source: Unexpectedly, co-translational signal-peptide cleavage of M26P gp160 significantly altered the oxidative folding pathway; folding intermediates acquired high compactness more quickly during synthesis (Figure 7A, Cells NR).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by non-reducing gel analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: The single large band of M26P implies the presence of long-distance disulfide bonds between 3 clusters.
source: In contrast, the single large band of M26P implies the presence of long-distance disulfide bonds between these 3 clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from limited proteolysis data in Figure 7C.

claim: Wild-type and M26P gp120 contain a similar set of disulfide bonds and a similar conformation after folding.
source: As we found no significant difference in the fragments after reduction, we concluded that both wild-type and M26P contained a similar set of disulfide bonds and a similar conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from limited proteolysis data in Figure 7D.

claim: Antibody A32, which recognizes a 3D epitope in the inner domain of gp120 around disulfide 54–74, showed a significant decrease in recognition of M26P.
source: Antibody A32, which recognizes a 3D epitope in the inner domain of gp120 around disulfide 54–74, showed a significant decrease in recognition of M26P (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by immunoprecipitation in Figure 7E-F.

claim: Antibody D7324, which recognizes an epitope near the disulfide bond in gp41, showed a significant decrease in M26P recognition.
source: Misfolding was not limited to gp120, as antibody D7324, which recognizes an epitope near the disulfide bond in gp41, also showed a significant decrease in M26P recognition (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by immunoprecipitation in Figure 7E-F.

claim: Co-translational signal-peptide cleavage resulted in localized misfolding in gp160.
source: We concluded that co-translational signal-peptide cleavage resulted in localized misfolding in gp160.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by antibody recognition data.

claim: M26P virus exhibited a slight delay in replication compared to wild-type virus, with virus levels being significantly lower at days 3 and 4.
source: M26P virus exhibited a slight delay in replication compared to wild-type virus, with virus levels being significantly lower at days 3 and 4, although the M26P mutant caught up with the wild-type virus at day 7.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by replication assays in Figure 8A.

claim: When mixed at a 1:1 ratio the wild-type virus had outcompeted M26P virus by day 4 and the M26P mutant was only present as a minority variant at day 35.
source: When mixed at a 1:1 ratio the wild-type virus had outcompeted M26P virus by day 4 and the M26P mutant was only present as a minority variant at day 35.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by competition assays in Figure 8B.

claim: When added in a ten-fold excess, the M26P mutant dominated the population at day 4, but again only formed a minority variant by day 35.
source: Moreover, when added in a ten-fold excess, the M26P mutant dominated the population at day 4, but again only formed a minority variant by day 35.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by competition assays in Figure 8B.

claim: The M26P mutant has a selective disadvantage to the wild-type virus.
source: These data indicate that the M26P mutant has a selective disadvantage to the wild-type virus.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from competition assay data.

claim: M26P JR-FL pseudo-virus was almost non-infectious compared to wild-type JR-FL pseudo-virus.
source: While wild-type JR-FL pseudo-virus readily infected target cells, M26P pseudo-virus was almost non-infectious (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by infectivity assays in Figure 8D.

claim: LAI pseudo-virus containing the Ig κ and cystatin signal peptides were significantly less infectious than wild-type LAI pseudo-virus.
source: We also compared the infectivity of LAI pseudo-virus containing the Ig κ and cystatin signal peptides (Figure 8E) and found them to be significantly less infectious than wild-type LAI pseudo-virus.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by infectivity assays in Figure 8E.

claim: Delayed cleavage of the signal peptide contributes to maximizing production of functional gp160.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that delayed cleavage of the signal peptide contributes to maximizing production of functional gp160 and that co-translational signal-peptide cleavage results in fast folding of lower-quality gp160.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by functional assays.

claim: Co-translational signal-peptide cleavage results in fast folding of lower-quality gp160.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that delayed cleavage of the signal peptide contributes to maximizing production of functional gp160 and that co-translational signal-peptide cleavage results in fast folding of lower-quality gp160.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by folding and functional assays.

claim: The dramatically delayed cleavage of the signal peptide of HIV-1 gp160 functions as folding regulator to ensure correct formation of disulfide bonds and functional structure.
source: We found that the dramatically delayed cleavage of the signal peptide of HIV-1 gp160 functions as folding regulator to ensure correct formation of disulfide bonds and functional structure.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data throughout the results section.

claim: This delayed cleavage is evolutionarily conserved across HIV-1 subtypes and is important for viral function.
source: This delayed cleavage is evolutionarily conserved across HIV-1 subtypes and is important for viral function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by sequence conservation and functional data.

claim: Secondary structure in the form of an alpha helix extends through the cleavage site preventing early access and cleavage by signal peptidase.
source: Secondary structure in the form of an alpha helix extends through the cleavage site preventing early access and cleavage by signal peptidase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural predictions and mutagenesis data.

claim: Uncleaved gp120 transiently resides in the ER as a signal-anchored type-II transmembrane protein with the cleavage site shielded by membrane phospholipids.
source: Uncleaved gp120 hence transiently resides in the ER as a signal-anchored type-II transmembrane protein with the cleavage site shielded by membrane phospholipids.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by FRAP and carbonate extraction data.

claim: The signal peptide acts a quality-control mechanism to ensure that gp160 exits the ER in an optimally folded form.
source: The integral-membrane intermediate is retained in the ER, and we here suggest that the signal peptide acts a quality-control mechanism to ensure that gp160 exits the ER in an optimally folded form.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from the functional consequences of early cleavage.

claim: Forced co-translational cleavage by insertion of a helix-breaking proline in the signal peptide led to changes in gp120 folding and reduced Env function.
source: Forced co-translational cleavage by insertion of a helix-breaking proline in the signal peptide led to changes in gp120 folding and reduced Env function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Proteases prefer loops and disfavor α-helices and β-sheets.
source: Proteases prefer loops and disfavor α-helices and β-sheets.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and represents established knowledge about protease specificity.

claim: NMR studies of E.coli signal peptidase in complex with alkaline phosphatase signal peptide revealed that the cleavage region adopted a poorly structured 'U-turn' shape.
source: NMR studies of E.coli signal peptidase in complex with alkaline phosphatase signal peptide revealed that the cleavage region adopted a poorly structured 'U-turn' shape (De Bona et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: A database of all verified signal peptides from Archaea to mammals shows ~20% of all cleavable signal peptides containing at least one proline in the −1 to −5 position relative to the cleavage site.
source: Enrichment of proline near signal-peptide cleavage sites is not limited to E. coli: a database of all verified signal peptides from Archaea to mammals shows ~20% of all cleavable signal peptides containing at least one proline in the −1 to −5 position relative to the cleavage site (Choo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Gp160 sequences are virtually devoid of proline in the −1 to −5 position relative to the cleavage site.
source: Gp160 sequences are virtually devoid of proline in that position (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by sequence analysis in Table 1.

claim: Ninety-five percent of all analyzed gp160 sequences contain M26 or I26 with only 5 sequences out of >4100 containing a proline in the −1 to −5 position.
source: Ninety-five percent of all analyzed sequences contain M26 or I26 with only 5 sequences out of >4100 containing a proline in the −1 to −5 position (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by sequence analysis in Table 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A sequence with similar signal-peptide/anchor probabilities may function as a transient signal anchor.
source: We show here that a signal peptide with mixed probabilities may well function as a transient signal anchor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data showing gp160 signal peptide acts as both.

claim: Tethering of the protease domain of the Semliki Forest virus capsid protein to the membrane via a non-cleavable signal anchor resulted in more efficient folding.
source: Tethering of the protease domain of the Semliki Forest virus capsid protein to the membrane via a non-cleavable signal anchor resulted in more efficient folding (Kowarik et al., 2002), and we propose that tethering gp120 might be similarly beneficial for gp120 folding.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In-silico folding simulations of knotted proteins demonstrated that efficiency of knot-domain formation was enhanced by tethering of the N-terminus.
source: In-silico folding simulations of knotted proteins demonstrated that efficiency of knot-domain formation was enhanced by tethering of the N-terminus (Soler and Faísca, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The M26P mutant immediately collapses into a more compact, disulfide-bonded state leading to a substantially more heterogeneously folded gp160 population.
source: In the context of gp160 this can be illustrated by our finding that the M26P mutant immediately collapses into a more compact, disulfide-bonded state leading to a substantially more heterogeneously folded gp160 population.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Post-translational cleavage of gp160 restricts conformational freedom, thereby preventing the initial collapse, and increases folding fidelity.
source: Post-translational cleavage of gp160 restricts conformational freedom, thereby preventing the initial collapse, and increases folding fidelity while ultimately allowing release from its tether, which is essential for its role in viral infectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from experimental data.

claim: Five out of ten conserved disulfide bonds are required for signal-peptide cleavage of gp160.
source: Previously, we have shown that signal-peptide cleavage requires folding and N-glycosylation of gp120 (Land et al., 2003), and that five out of ten conserved disulfide bonds are required for cleavage (van Anken et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Crystal structures of gp120 show that it adopts a hairpin conformation, with its N- and C-termini in close proximity.
source: Crystal structures of gp120 show that it adopts a hairpin conformation, with its N- and C-termini in close proximity (Garces et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: A late folding event (possibly integration of the N- and C-termini) likely triggers the conformational change in the N-terminus, allowing cleavage to occur.
source: Given that the far N-terminus is a β-strand in the native protein whereas our studies have suggested this region to be α-helical early on (which prevents co-translational cleavage), a late folding event (possibly integration of the N- and C-termini) likely triggers the conformational change in the N-terminus, allowing cleavage to occur.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from structural and experimental data.

claim: Co-translational signal-peptide cleavage caused localized misfolding in gp41 and in the inner domain of gp120.
source: As the association between subunits gp120 and gp41 involves gp120's N-terminus, it is appropriate that this conserved interface suffered from early cleavage; we found that co-translational signal-peptide cleavage caused localized misfolding in gp41 and in the inner domain of gp120.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by antibody recognition data.

claim: Strain-specific differences in stability of subunit association may be the reason why the effect of a heterologous signal peptide on gp160 function has been controversial.
source: Because the stability of the gp120/gp41 association differs substantially between HIV-1 strains this may explain the more dramatic impact of the M26P mutation in the context of the JR-FL isolate versus LAI. Strain-specific differences in stability of subunit association may be the reason why the effect of a heterologous signal peptide on gp160 function has been controversial thus far.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from experimental observations.

claim: As few as 9–14 native trimers on the virion surface suffice for infection.
source: Although as few as 9–14 native trimers on the virion surface suffice for infection (Zhu et al., 2006; Klasse, 2007), suboptimal Env trimers may require increased density for function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Hydrophobicity of prokaryotic signal peptides or in yeast proteins determines whether protein translocation is SRP-dependent or independent.
source: Hydrophobicity of prokaryotic signal peptides (Valent et al., 1997; Lee and Bernstein, 2001) or in yeast proteins (Ng et al., 1996) determines whether protein translocation is SRP-dependent or independent and generally the targeting efficiency of a signal peptide regulates expression levels.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Gp160 shows increased expression over the course of infection when the N-terminal charges in the signal peptide decrease.
source: Gp160 for instance shows increased expression over the course of infection when the N-terminal charges in the signal peptide decrease (Li et al., 1994; da Silva et al., 2011; Asmal et al., 2011; Gnanakaran et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Low efficiency in targeting may result in dual localization of the mature protein, which in the case of calreticulin gives rise to functional ER-lumenal and cytosolic pools.
source: Low efficiency in targeting may result in dual localization of the mature protein, which in the case of calreticulin gives rise to functional ER-lumenal and cytosolic pools (Shaffer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Actively tuning translocation efficiency of distinct sets of proteins allows the cell to react to ER stress.
source: Actively tuning translocation efficiency of distinct sets of proteins allows the cell to react to ER stress (Kang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Signal peptides may influence topology of the mature protein, as was shown for the human prion protein, PrP.
source: In addition to targeting, signal peptides may influence topology of the mature protein, as was shown for the human prion protein, PrP (Ott and Lingappa, 2004; Hegde et al., 1998), or they may regulate folding [e.g. gp160, US11, and EspP (Rehm et al., 2001; Szabady et al., 2005)].
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Signal peptides function as specialized, membrane-bound versions of soluble pro-peptides that function as intramolecular chaperones before their removal.
source: In this sense, they are specialized, membrane-bound versions of soluble pro-peptides that function as intramolecular chaperones before their removal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: After completion of synthesis, unprocessed deglycosylated gp120, with its signal peptide still attached (Ru) runs as a single band of ~70 kDa.
source: After completion of synthesis, unprocessed deglycosylated gp120, with its signal peptide still attached (Ru) runs as a single band of ~70 kDa (Land et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A, with citation to previous work.

claim: After a 60-min chase, a second band with increased mobility appears, representing signal-peptide-cleaved gp120 (Rc).
source: After a 60-min chase, a second band with increased mobility appears, representing signal-peptide-cleaved gp120 (Rc).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild-type HA and signal-peptide-swapped HA (gp120-HA) both ran as a single band on the gel.
source: Both wild-type and signal-peptide-swapped HA (gp120-HA) ran as a single band on the gel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GFP attached to the gp160 signal peptide was correctly targeted to the ER and accumulated in the ER due to the engineered retrieval signal KDEL.
source: As expected, GFP attached to the gp160 signal peptide was correctly targeted to the ER and accumulated in the ER due to the engineered retrieval signal KDEL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B SP+1, SP+10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of one residue of mature gp160 sequence linking the signal peptide and GFP (SP+1) resulted in a single band of GFP that migrated at the same position as control, GFP-KDEL.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed a single band of GFP when one residue of mature gp160 sequence linked the signal peptide and GFP (SP+1), which migrated at the same position as control, GFP-KDEL (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of four more residues of mature gp160 (SP+5) delayed the processing and resulted in signal-cleaved and uncleaved GFP species.
source: Addition of four more residues of mature gp160 (SP+5) delayed the processing and resulted in signal-cleaved and uncleaved GFP species.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Signal-peptide cleavage of the GFP-reporter constructs was not progressive.
source: Pulse-chase experiments showed that cleavage only occurred during the pulse-labeling period and not anymore after synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating that signal-peptide cleavage of the GFP-reporter constructs was not progressive.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Results for both 93IN101 SP+1 and SP+10 were comparable to those of HXB2, with efficient processing of SP+1 and delayed processing of SP+10.
source: Despite the low sequence similarity between the two isolates (Figure 3B), results for both 93IN101 SP+1 and SP+10 were comparable to those of HXB2, with efficient processing of SP+1 and delayed processing of SP+10.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Positions 39 and 40 were poorly glycosylated and thus located close to the ER membrane.
source: Positions 39 and 40 were poorly glycosylated and thus located close to the ER membrane (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The active site of signal peptidase is predicted to be 0.4–1.1 nm beyond the membrane surface.
source: The active site of signal peptidase is predicted to be 0.4–1.1 nm beyond the membrane surface (Liang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: When the gp160 signal peptide was tested with the impact of the mature HA sequence, separation between the H- and C-region visibly improved and cleaved signal-peptide probability increased to a near perfect 0.936.
source: SignalP analysis further corroborated our biochemical findings that the downstream residues of the mature gp120 influence probability of signal-peptide cleavage. When we tested the impact of the mature HA sequence on the gp160 signal peptide, separation between the H- and C-region visibly improved and cleaved signal-peptide probability increased to a near perfect 0.936 (Figure 6A), consistent with our experimental findings (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The overall signal of EndoH-sensitive cell-associated M26P gp160 and kinetics of gp120 shedding were comparable to wild-type type protein.
source: The overall signal of EndoH-sensitive cell-associated M26P gp160 and kinetics of gp120 shedding were comparable to wild-type type protein (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No difference was detected in aggregation or degradation of wild-type versus M26P gp160.
source: We did not detect any difference in aggregation or degradation of wild-type versus M26P gp160.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claim: A second, faster-migrating band of M26P (asterisk) was identified as cytosolic and attributed to suboptimal targeting to the ER due to weaker SRP binding.
source: A second, faster-migrating band of M26P (asterisk) was identified as cytosolic and attributed to suboptimal targeting to the ER due to weaker SRP binding: it did not change between reducing and non-reducing gels (Figure 7A, asterisk), or when DTT was removed from cells (Figure 7B, asterisk), indicating that it did not form disulfide bonds, it still contained the signal peptide, but did not contain the ~25 GlcNAc moieties that are left after deglycosylation with Endo H.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental observations in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Despite increased rate of compaction, the appearance of the distinct native (NT) band and shedding of M26P gp120 from gp41 took as long as for wild-type gp160.
source: Despite this increased rate of compaction, the appearance of the distinct native (NT) band and shedding of M26P gp120 from gp41 took as long as for wild-type gp160 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: M26P was digested into a slightly larger number of fragments, indicative of subtle conformational differences and more conformational heterogeneity than wild-type gp120.
source: M26P was digested into a slightly larger number of fragments, indicative of subtle conformational differences and more conformational heterogeneity than wild-type gp120.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from limited proteolysis data in Figure 7C.

claim: The three disulfide-linked diffuse bands from wild-type gp120 indicated that the protease had cleaved between 3 clusters of relatively local disulfide bonds, most likely between the variable loops.
source: The three disulfide-linked diffuse bands from wild-type gp120 indicated that the protease had cleaved between 3 clusters of relatively local disulfide bonds, most likely between the variable loops.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from limited proteolysis data.

claim: At the end of the 2-h chase both M26P and wild-type gp120 were highly protease resistant under non-reducing conditions.
source: Strikingly, at the end of the 2-h chase both M26P and wild-type gp120 were highly protease resistant under non-reducing conditions (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In both natively-folded proteins the cleavage must have primarily occurred within the variable loops as this would allow disulfide bonds to hold the structure intact.
source: As before, these large fragments dissociated into well-defined bands upon reduction (Figure 7D, R), indicating that in both natively-folded proteins the cleavage must have primarily occurred within the variable loops as this would allow disulfide bonds to hold the structure intact.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from limited proteolysis data in Figure 7D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation with CD4-IgG did not show a difference between wild-type and M26P gp160.
source: Immunoprecipitation with CD4-IgG did not show a difference between wild-type and M26P gp160 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: This misfolding was not sufficient to cause M26P to be retained in the ER or degraded.
source: This misfolding however, was not sufficient to cause M26P to be retained in the ER or degraded.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.
